title: Mikasa: lunch aboard the flagship and the problem of supply
dek: During the blockade of Port Arthur, 156 people aboard Mikasa suffered food poisoning. The shortage of food supply ships was recognised as a problem of that war, yet the fleet’s first dedicated food supply ship did not enter service until 1924.

sections.title: The flagship off Port Arthur
paragraphs: During the Russo-Japanese War, the battleship Mikasa took part in blockade operations off Port Arthur. She was an armoured Japanese warship and the flagship of the Combined Fleet—the ship carrying its commander. The Russian squadron was in its base; the Japanese ships operated outside it. They too needed an anchorage where they could undergo maintenance and replenish supplies. From 10 May 1904, Mikasa was undergoing maintenance at a forward base among the islands south of China’s Liaodong Peninsula.
The ship was still there on 30 May. Japanese historian Akinori Ishihara described that day’s lunch and the food poisoning that followed in his study of naval supply.

Rice and barley, soup with dried radish and tea were on the breakfast menu. More rice for lunch, with stewed canned salmon and seaweed, pickles and barley tea. For dinner, hardtack and roast beef with potatoes. At an anchorage where fresh food was scarce, Ishihara considers this a fairly ordinary menu.

sections.title: After lunch
paragraphs: The canned salmon had spoiled: its storage life had been exceeded. After lunch, 156 people aboard Mikasa fell ill. This happened on the flagship, at its own forward base, and the cause was food from the ship’s menu.

Food poisoning also occurred aboard other Japanese ships in May and June. Among the reported causes were canned goods, fried tofu (soybean curd) and mouldy bread; sometimes the offending food could not be identified. Aboard Mikasa, efforts were made to serve food that had been cooked: stewed, fried or boiled. The crew had to eat every day, despite all the difficulties of delivery and storage.

sections.title: Two supply ships and a long aftermath
paragraphs: At the start of the war, two auxiliary vessels, Matsuyama Maru and Fukuoka Maru, were prepared to supply food. Deliveries to the forward forces were planned roughly every six days. But the warships often operated in dispersed groups, and two supply vessels proved too few. From August 1904, Kotohira Maru and other ships were brought into this work.

The additional ships helped with transport, but they lacked enough equipment to preserve the food. They could not carry sufficient provisions. Even the few days’ voyage from the Japanese naval base at Sasebo to a forward base made it difficult to keep bread, vegetables, meat and fish fresh. Refrigeration technology already existed, but its installation aboard ships was only beginning.

The shortage of food supply vessels was recognised as one of the weaknesses of supply during the Russo-Japanese War. The auxiliary transports of 1904, however, were not yet the dedicated fleet food supply ships that appeared later. The first such ship in the Japanese navy, Mamiya, entered service in 1924. The second, Irako, followed on 5 December 1941.

Ishihara argues that, against the backdrop of the Japanese fleet’s victory at Tsushima in 1905, the supply shortcomings exposed by the war were not adequately reflected in subsequent naval policy. The dates behind that judgement are quite concrete: about twenty years passed between the war that revealed the shortage and Mamiya; another seventeen or so separated the commissioning of the first and second dedicated ships.

limitations: The lunch and number of people taken ill are described in Ishihara’s 2024 study. The original medical volume has not been checked separately; 156 counts people taken ill, not deaths. No causal link has been established between the spoilage of this batch of canned salmon and the shortage of ships.

The dates for Mamiya and Irako refer to dedicated fleet food supply ships. Auxiliary vessels were already supplying food in 1904. The assessment of how the navy absorbed the war’s lessons is Ishihara’s.

title: Money in Dairen: who could get a loan?
dek: Silver coins, Japanese banknotes and private credit firms. Bank clerk Sun Yaoting recalled a city with many kinds of money, where getting a loan was far from easy.

sections.title: A bank clerk in Dairen
paragraphs: Dairen was the name of Dalian under Japanese rule. Different kinds of money circulated in this trading city, yet an ordinary Chinese resident found it difficult to obtain a bank loan. Sun Yaoting recalled what people paid with, and who could borrow.
He had lived in Dalian since childhood and worked in banking from 1930. Starting as an apprentice and clerk, he eventually rose to senior positions. He knew the city’s banking life from the inside.

He names his workplace as Longkou, a joint Japanese-Chinese bank. He left an address too: Tianjin Street, as it was called when his account was recorded. Mergers and new bank names followed. Sun later described all this in the second issue of Materials on the History of Dalian.

sections.title: Silver and paper gold
paragraphs: His list includes silver coins, small silver coins, copper money and banknotes. He calls the Japanese paper money jinpiao, 金票. There is gold in the name, but these were notes, not gold coins.

Japanese banknotes predominated, Sun says. Chinese banks also issued paper money, but local issues required permission from the Japanese authorities and could serve only as temporary means of payment.

sections.title: Money in the city, money for its people
paragraphs: Sun describes Dairen as a city of manufacturing and trade with a constant need for money. Those seeking loans turned to the banks. But for an ordinary Chinese resident, he recalled, getting a bank loan was difficult: without adequate security—guarantees that the money would be repaid—there was little chance.

Loans were also available from qianzhuang, 钱庄, traditional private credit firms. They too required security and, Sun says, charged more interest than the banks. He writes separately about private moneylenders operating outside both banks and qianzhuang. In his judgement, an expensive loan could bring ruin in a short time.

limitations: Pages 49–53 of the library PDF were used, not the whole article. The publication date of the collection’s second issue has not been established. Tianjin Street is the name given by the memoirist; the exact building has not been identified.

This is a bank clerk’s later account, with pronounced anticolonial and class-based judgements, rather than a picture of all Chinese residents’ experience. Exact interest rates are not given here: their basis of calculation has not been checked. Currency circulation under Japanese rule cannot be applied to Russian Dalny or to Russian prices in 1913.
